sections.authorBiography: William Shakespeare was baptized in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564, the son of John Shakespeare, a glover and town official, and Mary Arden. He probably attended Stratford's grammar school, married Anne Hathaway in 1582, and had three children: Susanna and the twins Hamnet and Judith (Hamnet died aged eleven in 1596). By the early 1590s he was an actor and playwright in London; from 1594 he was a sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, who built the Globe theatre in 1599 and became the King's Men when James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603. He wrote or co-wrote about 38 plays and the Sonnets, and died in Stratford on 23 April 1616. Seven years later his fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell published 36 of his plays in the First Folio (1623).
sections.historicalContext: Romeo and Juliet was probably written around 1595, in the same years as A Midsummer Night's Dream, when Shakespeare was writing for the Lord Chamberlain's Men. The story was already well known in English: Arthur Brooke's long poem The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet (1562), based on a French version by Pierre Boaistuau of an Italian playla by Matteo Bandello (who drew on Luigi da Porto), was Shakespeare's main source. Shakespeare compressed Brooke's nine months into about four days, made Juliet younger (thirteen, "not fourteen"; Brooke's Juliet is sixteen) and greatly expanded Mercutio. In Elizabethan England fathers usually arranged the marriages of propertied daughters, and duelling and street brawls between rival retinues were a real worry to authorities. The play's love poetry draws on the fashion for sonnets in the 1590s: the lovers' first exchange is itself a sonnet.

publicationAndReception.publication: The play was printed in 1597 in a short First Quarto (sometimes called a "bad quarto") and in 1599 in a fuller Second Quarto "newly corrected, augmented, and amended," which is the basis of most modern texts; it was reprinted in the First Folio (1623). Modern editions, including the reading text here, combine readings from these early printings.
publicationAndReception.then: The play was popular in Shakespeare's lifetime, judging by its four quarto printings before the Folio. After the Restoration it fared less well: Samuel Pepys saw it on 1 March 1661/2 (1 March 1662 by modern reckoning) and called it "the worst that ever I heard in my life," and Thomas Otway turned it into a Roman play, Caius Marius (1679). David Garrick's version (1748) let Juliet wake before Romeo dies and held the stage for about a century.
publicationAndReception.now: It is one of the most performed and adapted of all plays and has been taught in American high schools for generations. Adaptations include Leonard Bernstein and Arthur Laurents's musical West Side Story (1957), Franco Zeffirelli's film (1968) and Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet (1996). Modern readers debate whether the play is about fate, about youthful impulsiveness, or about a violent society that destroys its children.

sections.overview: In Verona two great families, the Montagues and the Capulets, are locked in a feud so old that no one remembers its cause. Romeo, a Montague, slips into a Capulet party and meets Juliet, the Capulets' only daughter. The Prologue tells us at once how their story ends; the play shows how it gets there, in about four days.

sections.whyItMatters: Romeo and Juliet is the story of first love that the English-speaking world tells itself, and it is also a study of how a community's hatreds land on its young people. Students meet questions about loyalty to family, impulsive decisions, adults who fail to listen, and violence that escalates from words, all in some of the most famous poetry in English.

spoilerOverview.text: Romeo and Juliet marry secretly with the help of Friar Laurence and the Nurse. The next day Tybalt kills Mercutio and Romeo kills Tybalt, and the Prince banishes Romeo to Mantua. Capulet, not knowing of the marriage, insists Juliet marry Paris. The Friar gives her a potion that makes her seem dead; his letter to Romeo is stopped by a plague quarantine. Romeo hears she is dead, buys poison, kills Paris at the tomb and dies beside Juliet; she wakes, finds him dead and stabs herself. The families are reconciled over their children's bodies.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “A pair of star-cross’d lovers take their life” slowly and put it in my own words: The Chorus announces that a pair of lovers, crossed by the stars, will take their lives. Next, craft. I notice the sonnet form, a love-poem shape used to announce a tragedy, and "take their life," which means both "are born" and "kill themselves." The strongest word is “star-cross'd”: it means thwarted by the stars, so fate seems to be against them from the start. Then, effect. What does the Prologue tell us before the play begins? My answer: Shakespeare tells us the ending first, so we watch not to learn what happens but how and why; the line raises the play's question of whether fate or the characters' choices cause the deaths. segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet around 1595, adapting Arthur Brooke's 1562 poem, for audiences who believed in astrology and expected parents to arrange marriages. How might that context shape the play? Answer: Accept answers such as: belief in the stars made "star-crossed" meaningful; arranged marriage explains Capulet's anger at Juliet's refusal; Shakespeare turned a moral warning poem into a sympathetic tragedy.

lessonPlan.title: Romeo and Juliet unit
lessonPlan.author: William Shakespeare
lessonPlan.edition: Standard Ebooks edition (modern text drawing on the 1599 Second Quarto and the 1623 First Folio)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Romeo and Juliet.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Romeo and Juliet: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Romeo and Juliet has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to love and desire.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Romeo and Juliet. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this scene, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the scene on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the scene to love and desire.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the scene quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Romeo and Juliet.

objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the play in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the scene quizzes.

"Now old desire doth in his death-bed lie, / And young affection gapes to be his heir," and both lovers are "betwitched by the charm of looks.".

Both are bewitched by appearance. The evidence is “Alike betwitched by the charm of looks” (Act II, Prologue, Chorus). This develops love and desire: the Chorus questions how fast Romeo's love moved from Rosaline to Juliet. The words “betwitched” and “looks” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. "Now old desire doth in his death-bed lie, / And young affection gapes to be his heir," and both lovers are "betwitched by the charm of looks.".

Mercutio's mock spell. The evidence is “I conjure thee by Rosaline’s bright eyes” (Act II, Scene I, Mercutio). This develops love and desire: Mercutio reduces love to the body; the next scene will lift it to the stars. The words “conjure” and “bright” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He conjures Romeo "by Rosaline's bright eyes" and jokes that "Blind is his love and best befits the dark," not knowing Romeo has already left Rosaline behind.

Mercutio's nickname for Tybalt (Tybalt is a cat's name in fables). The evidence is “More than prince of cats, I can tell you” (Act II, Scene IV, Mercutio). This develops violence and the feud: Tybalt has sent Romeo a challenge; the comedy is shadowed by the coming duel. The words “prince” and “than” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Mercutio's mockery of Tybalt as "prince of cats" follows news of Tybalt's challenge, and Romeo plans the marriage ("Some means to come to shrift this afternoon") without knowing the challenge waits for him.

Moderation as the key to lasting love. The evidence is “Therefore love moderately; long love doth so” (Act II, Scene VI, Friar Laurence). This develops time and haste: the Friar again urges moderation even as he marries them within a day of meeting. The words “moderately” and “doth” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Before the ceremony the Friar says "These violent delights have violent ends" and urges "love moderately; long love doth so," a counsel the lovers cannot follow.

The Friar's warning. The evidence is “These violent delights have violent ends” (Act II, Scene VI, Friar Laurence). This develops time and haste: the Friar again urges moderation even as he marries them within a day of meeting. The words “delights” and “violent” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Before the ceremony the Friar says "These violent delights have violent ends" and urges "love moderately; long love doth so," a counsel the lovers cannot follow.

Romeo sees banishment as worse than death. The evidence is “Ha, banishment! be merciful, say ‘death” (Act III, Scene III, Romeo). This develops youth and age: the Friar's reason against Romeo's passion. The words “banishment” and “merciful” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He cries "be merciful, say 'death'" and insists "There is no world without Verona walls," until the Friar demands "Art thou a man?".

Juliet's feigned repentance. The evidence is “Where I have learn’d me to repent the sin / Of disobedient opposition” (Act IV, Scene II, Juliet). This develops time and haste: one day lost will prove fatal. The words “disobedient” and “opposition” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. She claims to "repent the sin / Of disobedient opposition," and Capulet, delighted, announces "We'll to church to-morrow," a day sooner.

Capulet's greeting. The evidence is “How now, my headstrong! where have you been gadding” (Act IV, Scene II, Capulet). This develops time and haste: one day lost will prove fatal. The words “headstrong” and “gadding” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. She claims to "repent the sin / Of disobedient opposition," and Capulet, delighted, announces "We'll to church to-morrow," a day sooner.

Death as bridegroom. The evidence is “Death is my son-in-law, Death is my heir” (Act IV, Scene V, Capulet). This develops death as bridegroom: Capulet's image makes the motif explicit. The words “heir” and “law” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Capulet says "Death is my son-in-law" and "All things that we ordained festival, / Turn from their office to black funeral.".

Romeo's defiance. The evidence is “Is it even so? then I defy you, stars” (Act V, Scene I, Romeo). This develops fate and choice: Romeo defies the stars, but in doing so fulfils the Prologue. The words “stars” and “then” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He cries "then I defy you, stars!" and resolves "Juliet, I will lie with thee to-night," buying poison from a man whose "poverty, but not my will, consents.".

finalPaper.title: Romeo and Juliet: final paper (formal literary analysis)

prompts.text: Analyze how William Shakespeare develops love and desire across Romeo and Juliet. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Romeo and Juliet and argue how its meaning changes over the play and why that change matters to fate and choice.
Analyze a central character's choices in Romeo and Juliet. Argue whether the play judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.

Two readers disagree about whether Romeo and Juliet finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of violence and the feud. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the act, scene and line (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

Thesis: Specific, arguable and precise; it organizes every section.
Clear and arguable, but broad in places.
States a topic or a summary more than an argument.
Evidence: Accurate, well-chosen quotations from across the work, all cited; meets the requirement.
Accurate and cited, but clustered in one part of the work.
Too few quotations, or some inaccurate or uncited.
Analysis: Explains how specific words, structure and devices create meaning; weighs a competing reading.
Explains the evidence, with some close reading.
Mostly summary; the link to the claim is asserted, not shown.
Organization: Each paragraph advances the argument; transitions show logic.
Order is loose; paragraphs repeat or drift.
Style and conventions: Formal, precise, present tense; MLA format; virtually error-free.
Formal with a few errors that do not obscure meaning.
Informal or error-prone in ways that distract.

finalPaper.exemplar: The cast list shows a city divided into camps, with only the Prince's kin standing outside the feud. The text makes this visible when it says “Montague and Capulet, heads of houses at variance with each other” (Dramatis Personae). "Montague and Capulet, heads of houses at variance" are paired as enemies, while Mercutio is "kinsman to the prince, and friend to Romeo": a neutral who will be pulled into the fight. A full paper would carry this reading through the beginning, middle and end, and answer the strongest competing reading.

criticalVoices.quote: Under his handling, it has become a glorious song of praise on that inexpressible feeling which ennobles the soul and gives to it its highest sublimity, and which elevates even the senses into soul, while at the same time it is a melancholy elegy on its inherent and imparted frailty; it is at once the apotheosis and the obsequies of love.
criticalVoices.speaker: August Wilhelm Schlegel, critic and translator of Shakespeare
criticalVoices.source: Lectures on Dramatic Art and Literature (1809-11), trans. John Black, Lecture XXV, Lecture XXV
criticalVoices.useNote: Final paper: Schlegel calls the play "at once the apotheosis and the obsequies of love." Test that claim against the whole play: where does it celebrate love, where does it mourn it, and which wins?
